chapters.title: Day 2 · Dover, Calais, Paris, the Alps — to Brindisi
chapters.hook: Verne wrote a novel about going round the world and then skipped Europe. Everything the book says about the next three days is seven lines in a notebook, and it takes twenty seconds to read.
chapters.recap: Yesterday in London, a gentleman named Phileas Fogg bet half his fortune that he could travel round the world in eighty days, and left at a quarter to nine at night with a French servant, Passepartout. Today we follow them to Dover, across the Channel, through Paris, under the Alps and down to the heel of Italy — and stop at everything they went past.

scenes.title: Day 2 · everything Verne wrote about the next three days
scenes.learning_goal: Know who Fogg is, what he bet, and that the whole crossing of Europe exists in the novel as seven timestamps; feel the size of the gap we are about to walk into.

narration.script:
Day two. If you have just joined us: in 1872 Jules Verne published a novel. A London gentleman named Phileas Fogg bets half his money that he can travel round the world in eighty days. He left London last night at a quarter to nine, with a French servant, Passepartout.

The route was printed in the newspaper on the night of the bet. The first line says: 'London to Suez, by way of Mont Cenis and Brindisi, by rail and steamboats — seven days.'

That is nearly all the novel says. Fogg keeps a notebook. The first line: 'Left London, Wednesday, October the second, at eight forty-five p.m.'

The last line: 'Sailed on the Mongolia, Saturday, at five p.m.'

Seven lines. Three thousand kilometres.

scenes.title: Dover — the train ran out to the ship
scenes.subtopic: 2 — Dover, and the hour and a quarter of open sea
scenes.learning_goal: Know that the boat train ran out along the Admiralty Pier so you stepped from carriage to deck, that the cliffs are chalk and France is 32 km off, and that the crossing was a byword for misery; feel cold air and open water.

narration.script:
Dover, and a night boat. Charles Dickens crossed here in 1863 and wrote about it. On the deck he watches the train come to him: 'A screech, a bell, and two red eyes come gliding down the Admiralty Pier.'

The railway ran out along the pier, over the water, to the ship. On Fogg's night the rails ran out along it too, so his train would have stopped beside the steamer. You stepped from the carriage onto the deck, without touching a street.

Above the harbour, the cliffs. Chalk, about a hundred metres high, and roughly a hundred million years old. France is thirty-two kilometres away. On a clear day you can see it. The French call this water la Manche — the sleeve. Verne never mentions any of this.

An hour and a quarter of open sea. Dickens again, about the other passengers: they 'lie about in melancholy bundles, as if they were sorted out for the laundress.' One man holds his umbrella up the whole way over.

Our pictures are daylight, and a lifetime late. Fogg crossed in the middle of the night.

scenes.title: Calais — the train this whole route exists for
scenes.learning_goal: Know that our train is the Indian Mail, that it could only run because rails reached Brindisi in 1865 and the canal opened in 1869, and that the first P&O sailing from Brindisi was two years before Fogg; feel the border arrive as a sound.

narration.script:
The boat comes in beside the railway station quay — le quai — and hands you to the train. Customs officers in green and grey. Touts shouting English the way the French hear it. Hot coffee at one in the morning.

This is the train. In French, la malle des Indes — the India mail. It runs from Calais to Brindisi to meet a ship. It exists because of three dates: rails reached the heel in 1865, the Suez Canal opened in 1869, and the first steamer left Brindisi for India in October 1870. Two years before Fogg.

In the novel, when the bank is robbed, detectives go to six ports. Brindisi is one, and nobody needs it explained.

One last thing about the night train to Paris. It runs through Amiens — where Jules Verne had been living for a year, writing this book.

scenes.title: Paris — eighty minutes, through the window of a cab
scenes.subtopic: 4 — Paris: eighty minutes, in the rain
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Passepartout is a Parisian who is driven across his own city between two stations without stopping, and that neither station looked the way we picture it; feel the comedy before the sadness.

narration.script:
Twenty past seven, Thursday morning. The train comes into the Gare du Nord — the North station. Passepartout is a Parisian. He left France five years ago, and last night he was hoping for exactly this. It would do his eyes good, he thinks, to see Paris once more.

He gets eighty minutes. The next train leaves from the Gare de Lyon, four kilometres across the city. The two of them cross Paris in a horse-cab, in the rain.

Two dates while we cross. The station he arrives at is eight years old: this front was finished in 1864. The one he leaves from had burned down sixteen months earlier, in the Commune. And the Gare de Lyon everybody photographs, with the clock tower, is from 1900. Nobody in 1872 ever saw it.

Eighty minutes. He does not get out.

scenes.title: The hole through the mountain
scenes.learning_goal: Know that the Fréjus tunnel was dug from both ends between 1857 and 1870, opened thirteen months before Fogg's train, and was the longest in the world until 1882 — and that a machine is why it took thirteen years, not seventy-one.

narration.script:
That was the way over. This is the way through.

They started in 1857, from both ends, with nothing in the middle: no shaft, no daylight, two teams walking towards each other under the mountain. By hand, people said, it would have taken about seventy-one years.

So Germain Sommeiller's men used a machine he had to invent first — a compressed-air drill, ten of them held in one frame. And the air that drove the drills came out of them and became the air the men breathed.

The two ends met on the twenty-sixth of December, 1870. The tunnel opened on the seventeenth of September, 1871 — thirteen months before Fogg's train. Nobody had ever made a hole this long, and nobody made a longer one until 1882.

And here it is today. Italians call it simply il traforo — the tunnel. Same arch, same hole, still the way through.

scenes.title: A fourth date — and the only one he goes through
scenes.learning_goal: See the tunnel in section and the four dates that made the eighty days thinkable; know that Fréjus is the only one Fogg physically travels through — and that the same tunnel reopened in March 2025.

narration.script:
Here is the mountain, cut in half. The thin line over the top is the way they went the year before. The straight line under it is the way we are going, and it is dark the whole way.

On day one we lit three dates. The Suez Canal, 1869. The American railway, joined in 1869. The last railway link across India, 1870. Three doors, opened within ten months. They made eighty days possible.

Here is a fourth. The seventeenth of September, 1871. It is the only one of the four that Fogg actually travels through. It is even in the first line of his printed route — 'by way of Mont Cenis and Brindisi'. He goes through it in the dark, asleep, and the book never mentions it.

One more thing, and this one you can book. The same tunnel is still the way through. A rockfall closed the line for nineteen months. It reopened on the thirty-first of March, 2025.

scenes.learning_goal: Find three things at Porta Nuova without being told where to point — the name, the clock, and the fact that the rails end here — and learn that the world's oldest museum of ancient Egypt is a walk away from a man on his way to Egypt.

narration.script:
Twenty-five to seven in the morning, in Turin. Fogg has forty-five minutes. Three things to find. First: read the name across the front of the station. Second: find the clock. Third: look at how the building closes the end of the square — the rails stop here, and everyone has to turn round.

Torino Porta Nuova. When Fogg waited here, the station was four years old. And the city had just lost something too: Turin was the capital of Italy from 1861 to 1865, and had been an ordinary city again for seven years.

Now the pin. About nine hundred metres in that direction — you cannot see it from here — is the oldest museum in the world devoted only to ancient Egypt. It was founded in 1824. Fogg is on his way to Egypt. He has forty-five minutes.

scenes.title: The end of the Appian Way
scenes.learning_goal: Find the base of the lost second column and the steps down to the water, and know that Rome's road east ends 150 m from the quay where Britain's mail for India was put on a ship.

narration.script:
Last stop before the sea. Two things to find. Above you are le colonne romane — the Roman columns. Only one is still standing. Find the other: there is a base, and nothing else. Then find the steps down to the water.

narration.script: Four o'clock, Saturday afternoon. One hour. The quay is still called the stazione marittima — the harbour station, where the train meets the ship. And here is the Mongolia. scenes.title: Souvenir — Fogg's notebook, and yours
scenes.learning_goal: Take away the seven lines with a blank column beside them, and one train that can still be booked; feel quiet satisfaction at having stopped where Fogg did not.

narration.script:
Six days from here, at Suez, Fogg finds he is exactly on time. Then Verne writes the sharpest sentence in the book about him. Fogg eats breakfast in his cabin and never thinks of looking at the town — 'one of those Englishmen who are wont to see foreign countries through the eyes of their domestics.'

Your souvenir is his notebook: seven lines, three thousand kilometres, an empty column headed 'what I saw'. On the back, the one thing you can still book: Paris to Turin, through Sommeiller's tunnel.
